selected_decision.what_happened: Alaska Energy Authority CEO Curtis Thayer publicly refuted DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV LLC's federal regulatory filing claim that its proposed 100-megawatt underwater AI data center project (roughly 350 tidal turbines and 66 subsea server 'hives' off Nikiski) was designed to tie into AEA's ongoing $400 million Cook Inlet PowerLink submarine transmission project, stating AEA had never been contacted by the company and that the filing's facts were 'dead wrong.'
selected_decision.the_binary: Whether AEA would let DeepGreen's claim of a public-infrastructure partnership stand unchallenged in the federal permitting record, versus publicly and specifically disavowing it. Thayer chose public refutation over silence or tacit accommodation.
selected_decision.ak_consequence: Energy/infrastructure sector: Thayer's public refutation puts a credibility marker on DeepGreen's 100 MW underwater AI data center proposal as it attempts to tie into AEA's $400 million ratepayer- and state-backed Cook Inlet PowerLink line, shaping how FERC and Kenai Peninsula stakeholders weigh the DeepGreen application during the federal comment/intervention period that opened September 4, 2026.
selected_decision.debatable_axis: Pro: protects the integrity of the federal regulatory record and AEA's reputation, and guards against a speculative, un-vetted developer invoking a $400M public infrastructure investment as leverage without any actual coordination. Con: a blunt public rebuke of a project pitched as a clean, tidal-powered, grid-stabilizing data center could read as reflexive gatekeeping at a moment when the state is actively courting data-center investment and Chugach Electric has said it needs large new loads to spread fixed costs across a shrinking customer base.

structural_read: This is a small, sharp episode in Alaska's emerging data-center gold rush, and it's worth taking seriously precisely because it's small: an East Coast-backed shell company filed with FERC claiming a working relationship with the state's Railbelt transmission authority that, per AEA's own CEO, does not exist. Thayer's on-the-record correction is a legitimate exercise of institutional authority. It protects the federal record from an unverified claim and puts future speculative filers on notice that Alaska's public power infrastructure isn't a plug-and-play backdrop for AI data-center pitches. That said, the underlying tension is real and unresolved: Alaska's utilities are simultaneously signaling they want large new industrial loads (including AI infrastructure) to help underwrite grid costs, and Thayer's rebuke, however factually justified, lands as a public no rather than a public 'let's talk.' Whether AEA treats this as a one-off correction or the opening move in a more adversarial posture toward data-center developers will say a lot about how Alaska actually competes for this investment class.
forward_implication: FERC's Project No. 15423-000 comment and intervention period opened September 4, 2026. Watch whether AEA files formal comments or moves to intervene, whether DeepGreen amends or withdraws the PowerLink interconnection claim, and how Kenai Peninsula Borough and Cook Inlet stakeholders respond during the window. Also watch whether Thayer's rebuke becomes a template for how Railbelt utilities and authorities respond to other speculative data-center developers (North Slope, Mat-Su) invoking public infrastructure without direct engagement.
